Concrete designed for this shore

A concrete that would serve for generations inland can fail early here. The reason is chloride. The sea wind delivers it every day, it works its way through the cover to the reinforcement, and the steel begins to rust. Rust takes up more room than steel. The concrete cracks from the inside.

The Indian code for concrete, IS 456, grades this danger by exposure. A structure open to coastal air is in severe exposure. One reached by sea spray is in very severe exposure. The tidal zone is extreme. For each grade the code asks for a stronger and denser concrete, and more of it between the steel and the air.

Exposure, as IS 456 defines it Minimum grade Maximum water to cement ratio Minimum cement content Nominal cover to steel

Those are minimums for reinforced concrete, and your designer’s specification governs. We treat them as the floor and not the target.

Blended cements and mineral additions
Fly ash and slag make a denser paste that chloride finds harder to cross. They also lower the heat of a large pour.
Corrosion inhibitors
Added to the mix where the design calls for them.
Cover
Set with proper cover blocks of the same strength as the concrete, and checked before every pour. A bar that sits 20 mm too close to the face has lost most of its protection.
Compaction
Honeycombing is a door left open. Vibrators, and people who know how to use them.
Curing
Kept wet for at least seven days, and at least ten where blended cement is used. In the hot months, longer.

Our essay What salt does to concrete tells the whole story.

  1. Materials are tested before they are used

    Cement, aggregates and reinforcement steel come from approved sources and are tested at NABL-accredited laboratories.

  2. The mix is designed, then proved

  3. A request for inspection is raised

    Reinforcement, cover, formwork, embedments and levels are offered to your engineer. Nothing is poured over until the request is signed.

  4. The pour is planned as an operation

  5. Cubes are cast and the pour is logged

Why a machine foundation is different

A building foundation carries a load that sits still. A machine foundation carries a load that moves. A crusher hammers. A mill rotates out of balance by design. A fan runs at one speed for years and finds any weakness in whatever holds it.

The designer answers this with mass and stiffness, proportioned so that the block’s own natural frequency stays well away from the machine’s running speed. Indian practice follows the IS 2974 series for machine foundations, and the machine’s maker supplies the loads.

Our part is to build exactly what was designed. On this kind of structure “nearly” is the same as “wrong”.

The six things that decide it

  1. The ground is seen before it is covered

    We excavate to founding level and offer the stratum to your engineer. In this district that may be limestone, marl or basalt, and they do not behave alike. A soft pocket or a void is dealt with now, not discovered later as a tilt.

  2. The block is poured as one

    A dynamic foundation is cast monolithic wherever the design allows. A cold joint in the wrong place is a plane along which a vibrating block can work itself apart. Where a joint cannot be avoided, the designer places it and we prepare it.

  3. The bolts are held by a template

    Anchor bolts, sleeves and pockets are set from a steel template fabricated to the maker’s foundation drawing. The template is surveyed into position, braced so that concrete cannot push it, and surveyed again before the pour and after it.

  4. The concrete can reach every corner

    These blocks are dense with steel. Before the pour we check that concrete can flow around every bolt and through every layer of bars, and we choose the mix, the pump and the vibrators to suit.

  5. The top is left for the grout

    The surface under each base plate is finished low and rough, ready for the grout that will make the final seat. See Alignment and grouting.

  6. It is cured before it is loaded

    The block gains its strength in the weeks after the pour. A machine is not set, and certainly not run, until the cubes say it may be.

What goes wrong, and how it is prevented

A bolt is out of position
The template is surveyed three times. The as-built bolt survey is handed to the erection team before the machine leaves its crate.
Honeycombing round the bolts
Mock-up of the congested zone where needed, the right slump, and a vibrator operator who knows the job.
A cold joint
Standby pump, standby supply and a pour plan that does not depend on luck.
Cracks from heat
Large blocks are treated as mass concrete.
The floor transmits vibration
The foundation is separated from the surrounding floor by the isolation joint the drawing shows, and the joint is kept clean.

  • Reinforcement and embedment inspection, signed before the pour
  • Bolt and pocket survey, before and after concreting

Where piles and rafts are needed

Inland, the builder’s problem is rock that is too hard. Along the shore it can be the opposite: marine clay, loose fill, or ground that was sea a generation ago.

Two answers are in common use. A raft spreads the load over a wide slab so that the pressure on the soil is small. Piles carry the load down past the weak layers to firm ground, and a pile cap ties the heads of the piles together under the structure.

Which to use is the designer’s decision, made on the soil investigation. Building it well is ours.

How a bored pile is made

Our network includes piling rigs for bored cast-in-situ piles, the kind covered by the IS 2911 series.

  1. Set out

    Each pile position is surveyed and marked. A pile in the wrong place cannot be moved.

  2. Bore

    The rig drills to the depth the design requires. The sides of the hole are held by a casing or by drilling fluid, so that they do not fall in.

  3. Check the base

    Depth is measured and the bottom is cleaned. The founding stratum is logged against the borehole data.

  4. Lower the cage

    The reinforcement cage goes in with spacers that guarantee its cover. Near this shore the ground water is saline, and the cover is the pile’s only protection.

  5. Concrete through a tremie

    Concrete is placed from the bottom upward through a pipe that stays buried in the fresh concrete, so that it displaces the fluid and never mixes with it. The pour is continuous.

  6. Cut off and test

    The head is trimmed to sound concrete. Piles are tested as the specification requires, for integrity and for load.

Pile caps and rafts

Once the piles are proved, the cap or raft is an exercise in heavy reinforcement and, often, in mass concrete.

Excavation and dewatering
Near the shore the water table is high. Pumps and a disposal route are part of the plan.
Pile heads
Broken down carefully to cut-off level, with the pile’s bars left projecting into the cap.
Blinding
A lean concrete layer that gives a clean, level surface to build on.
Reinforcement
Heavy bars, closely spaced, fixed to cover and inspected before the pour.
Concrete
Dense, durable and placed without a break.

What we watch for

A hole that collapses
Casing or fluid kept in control, and concreting begun without delay once the cage is in.
Soil in the concrete
The tremie stays buried. If the pour is interrupted, the pile is reported, not hidden.
A cage that floats or leans
Spacers, lifting points and a check on cage level during the pour.
Salt
Cover, dense concrete and tested water.

The problem with size

Cement gives off heat as it hardens. In a wall the heat escapes. In a block two metres thick it cannot. The core grows hot while the surface, open to the air, cools.

Hot concrete expands and cool concrete shrinks. When the difference between the heart of the block and its skin grows too large, the skin cracks. On this coast a crack is a road for chloride.

So a large pour is not an ordinary pour made bigger. It is an operation of its own. We have executed temperature-controlled pours of more than 1,000 cubic metres.

Keeping it cool

Less heat in the mix
Blended cements and mineral additions release their heat more slowly than ordinary cement. On this shore we want them for durability in any case.
Cool ingredients
Aggregates are shaded and sprayed. Mixing water is chilled, or part of it is replaced with ice, when the specification calls for a limit on placing temperature.
Night pours
In the hot months large pours begin in the evening. The concrete is cooler, and so are the people placing it.
Layers that stay alive
Concrete is placed in layers, each one covered by the next before it has begun to set, so that the block has no cold joints.
Insulation, not cooling, at the surface
It sounds wrong, but the surface is kept warm. The aim is a small difference between core and skin, not a cold skin.
Measurement
Thermocouples are cast into the block at its core and near its faces. Temperatures are logged until the peak has passed and the difference is safe.

The limit on the difference between core and surface is set by your designer. A figure of about 20 °C is common.

Keeping it continuous

A pour that stops is a pour that has failed. Everything about the logistics is planned to prevent a stop.

Before a mass pour begins

The arithmetic of a night

A pump placing 40 cubic metres an hour takes 25 hours to place 1,000. Each mixer carries about 6 cubic metres. If the batching plant is twenty minutes away, the round trip with loading and discharge is over an hour, and the pour needs eight or more mixers running without a break through the night and the following day.

One late mixer is a nuisance. Three late mixers is a cold joint. The plan is built so that neither happens.

You can try the numbers for your own pour in the concrete calculator.

Afterwards

Curing is longer for a mass pour than for an ordinary one, and it is recorded. Formwork and insulation come off when the thermocouples say so, and not when the programme would like.

The rock

Deccan Trap basalt is lava that cooled into a dense, dark, fine-grained stone. It is hard and it is blocky. It comes in flows, one on top of another, with weathered and fractured bands between them. South of Amreli it is cut by dykes of dolerite and rhyolite that are harder still.

Above it, along the shore, lies the miliolite limestone, which a good excavator can rip. Between them there is often marl.

A trench that begins in soil can pass through all three in a hundred metres. We have been digging here since 2015, and we know what to expect and where.

Why breakers, and not blasting

Blasting is fast in open country. Beside an operating plant it is another matter. It needs licences and a magazine. It needs the area cleared, and it stops work around it. It throws stone, and it shakes foundations that are carrying running machines.

Heavy hydraulic breakers avoid all of that. A 50-tonne excavator with a rock breaker fractures the toughest strata in place, a few metres from live equipment if need be, at any hour, with nothing to evacuate. Deep foundations and cable trenches are opened without waiting on blasting.

How a rock excavation is run

  1. Find what is buried first

    Cables, pipes and earthing run everywhere under a plant. Drawings are checked, the route is scanned, and trial pits are dug by hand where there is doubt. An excavation permit is taken before the first bucket.

  2. Strip and expose

    Soil and soft rock come off with the bucket. The top of hard rock is exposed and its level recorded jointly with your engineer.

  3. Break in benches

    The breaker works the rock in steps, from a free face, so that each blow has somewhere to send the stone.

  4. Load out as you go

    A second excavator loads tippers. Spoil leaves as the excavation advances, so that the work front never chokes.

  5. Trim to level

    The last few hundred millimetres are taken carefully. Over-break has to be filled with concrete, and that is money.

  6. Hand over

    Founding levels are surveyed and offered for inspection. Edges are barricaded and access is made safe.

Measuring what was dug

Soil and rock are paid at different rates, and where one ends and the other begins is the oldest argument in earthwork.

We do not leave it for the final bill. Levels are taken jointly before work starts, at the top of rock, and at the finish. The strata are classified jointly as they are exposed, with photographs. The measurement is agreed while the evidence is still open to the sky.

What we watch for

A dyke across the line
Harder than the basalt around it. Progress slows, and we tell you the day it is met.
Water
Rock excavations collect it. Pumps, sumps and a place to send the water.
Vibration near live plant
The breaker’s position and size are chosen with the neighbouring foundations in mind. Monitoring is arranged where your engineer asks for it.
The edge
Barricades, lights at night, a ladder in every pit, and no machine parked at the lip.
Dust
Water spray at the work face.

Roads that carry the load

A road fails from the bottom. The concrete on top is only as good as what lies under it, so we build upward in layers and prove each one before it is covered.

  1. Subgrade

    The natural ground is shaped and compacted. Soft spots are dug out and replaced. Where the soil swells when wet, it is treated or removed.

  2. Granular sub-base

    A layer of graded stone that spreads the load and drains freely.

  3. Lean concrete base

    A dry lean concrete layer, rolled, that gives the pavement a stiff and even bed.

  4. Pavement quality concrete

    The slab itself, of high-strength concrete, laid in panels. Steel dowels carry load from one panel to the next. Tie bars hold neighbouring lanes together.

  5. Joints, texture and curing

    Joints are sawn at the right hour, neither too early nor too late. The surface is textured for grip. Curing begins at once and is not cut short.

Rigid pavements of this kind are designed to the Indian Roads Congress guidelines. Thickness and joint spacing come from your designer and from the traffic the road must carry.

Building a road in a plant that cannot stop

A plant does not close a road so that it can be rebuilt. Trucks must keep moving while we work.

  • The road is built in halves, with traffic on the other half.
  • Diversions are signed, lit and marshalled.
  • Panels beside live traffic are protected until they have their strength.
  • Turning circles for trailers and bulkers are checked on the ground, not only on the drawing.

Drains shaped to the monsoon

Nearly all of this coast’s rain falls in four months, and much of it in a few days. A drain here is sized for the worst hour, not the average one.

Stormwater drains
Open and covered drains in reinforced concrete, laid to falls that follow the plant’s own topography.
Culverts and crossings
Under roads and rail sidings, strong enough for the traffic above them.
Cable trenches and ducts
Trenches with covers, duct banks and pull pits, built to the electrical drawing and kept dry.
Pits and sumps
With pumps where water has nowhere to go by gravity.
Kerbs, edges and hard shoulders
So that a tyre off the slab does not begin the road’s destruction.

What we watch for

Water under the slab

Vacuum-dewatered flooring

The method we use most is vacuum-dewatered flooring. Plants know it as VDF, or as Tremix after the company that made the equipment familiar.

The idea is simple. Concrete needs extra water to be workable, but every drop that is not needed for the chemistry leaves a void behind when it dries. Vacuum dewatering lets us place a workable concrete and then take the surplus water back out before it sets.

  1. Prepare the base

    The sub-base is compacted and levelled. A floor is only as flat as what it sits on.

  2. Set the panels

    Side forms are fixed to level, dividing the floor into bays. Dowels are placed where load must pass from one bay to the next.

  3. Place and vibrate

    Concrete is spread, compacted with poker vibrators and struck off with a screed vibrator running on the forms.

  4. Draw the water out

    Filter mats are laid over the fresh concrete and a vacuum pump draws surplus water through them. The slab soon stiffens enough to walk on.

  5. Float and trowel

    A power floater closes the surface and a power trowel finishes it hard and smooth. Where the duty is severe, a dry-shake floor hardener is worked into the top.

  6. Cut the joints and cure

    Joints are sawn within a day, then sealed. The floor is cured for its full period before it sees a wheel.

What the method gives

  • A denser, stronger surface than ordinary trowelled concrete
  • Less shrinkage, so less curling and cracking
  • Better resistance to abrasion
  • A floor that can be finished the same day it is poured

Where it is used

Bag godowns and packing plant floors. Clinker and raw material stores. Workshops and stores. Loading bays and hardstands. Container yards and warehouse floors for the port and its logistics parks.

Getting it right

Flatness
Forms set by level, checked before every bay.
Joints
Planned on a drawing, so that they fall away from wheel paths and line up with columns.
Curing
The step most often skipped, and the one that decides whether a floor dusts.
The edges
Bay edges and joint arrises are where a floor breaks first. They are compacted and finished with particular care.

How a silo ages

Salt
Chloride reaches the reinforcement, the steel rusts and swells, and the cover concrete is pushed off in sheets.
Load
Every filling presses outward on the wall. Every discharge shifts the pressure. Over years the hoop steel is worked hard.
Heat
Hot material inside and sea air outside pull the wall in two directions.
Wear
Flowing material scours the inside faces and the cone.

Repair without stopping the plant

A silo is rarely available to be emptied for months. We have carried out silo repairs that restored structural integrity without taking the plant offline, working on the outer face while the silo stayed in service.

  1. Assess

    With our engineering panel: visual survey, hammer sounding, cover measurement and whatever tests the engineer orders. The extent of the damage is mapped before a price is given.

  2. Access

    Scaffold or suspended platforms, designed and inspected, with a rescue plan. Most of this work is at height.

  3. Remove what has failed

    Loose and delaminated concrete is cut back to sound material and behind the bars.

    Rust is cleaned off. Bars that have lost section are supplemented. Protective coatings are applied where the repair system calls for them.

For local damage. Sound edges, a bonding coat and a repair material matched to the parent concrete.

Concrete sprayed at high velocity on to the prepared surface, over new mesh. It builds a dense new skin on a curved wall without formwork.

New concrete that does not grip the old is decoration. Surface preparation is inspected before anything is applied.

  3. Level and align

    Using precision levels and measuring instruments, the base is brought to the level, the position and the alignment on the maker’s drawing. The tolerances for this work are fine, and they are the maker’s, not ours.

  4. Record and offer for inspection

    Readings are written into a protocol. Your engineer and, where present, the maker’s representative sign it before any grout is mixed.

Then grout

  1. Choose the grout

    A non-shrink cementitious grout for most bases. An epoxy grout where the machine is highly dynamic or the maker requires it. The choice is in the specification or is made with our engineering panel.

  2. Build the formwork

    Tight, strong and sealed, with a head box on one side so that the grout flows under the plate by gravity.

  3. Pour from one side

    Continuously, in one direction, until grout appears on the far side. This pushes the air out ahead of it. Pouring from two sides traps air under the plate, and air does not carry load.

  4. Cure

    Kept wet and shaded. On a summer afternoon here an unprotected grout can lose its water before it has gained its strength.

  5. Tighten

    Anchor bolts are finally tightened only when the grout has reached the strength the maker specifies.

Voids under the plate
Grout poured from both sides, or allowed to stop. Tapping the plate afterwards tells the truth.
Grout that shrinks
The wrong material, too much water, or no curing.
A base that moved
Packers not secured, or bolts pulled up before the grout was hard.
A foundation that was not ready
Laitance left on, or a dry surface.

For eleven months or more a kiln turns. It is sixty or seventy metres of steel tube lined with brick, tilted a few degrees, and inside it the material reaches about 1,450 °C, a heat the steel shell could not survive without the brick. Then it is stopped, and it must cool before anyone can enter.

Why silos choke

Powder that sits against a wall takes up moisture and hardens. The hard layer narrows the silo and the outlets. Material begins to arch over the outlets or to hang on the walls. Capacity is lost first, then flow, and at last a discharge gate jams or a lump comes down and blocks the outlet altogether.

The cure is to bring the build-up down and clear it.

The danger

Silo cleaning has killed people in this industry, and the manner of it is always the same. Someone went in underneath material that then moved.

Stored powder behaves like a liquid when it is aerated. A hanging arch can collapse without warning. Our method starts from one rule, and the rule is not negotiable at any hour or under any pressure of production.

Nobody enters a silo below hanging material, and nobody stands on stored material. Build-up is brought down from above or from outside, with the people in a place where it cannot fall on them.

How we go about it

  1. Plan with the plant

    The condition of the silo, the level and the nature of the build-up, the access points and the method are agreed in writing.

  2. Isolate

    Feed, extraction, aeration and anything else that could move material is isolated, locked and tried.

  3. Test and ventilate

    The air is tested for oxygen and dust is allowed to settle.

  4. Work from above or from outside

    Through the roof and manholes, from platforms or with equipment lowered in, so that material falls away from the people.

  5. Clear the outlets

    As material comes down it is extracted, so that it does not rebuild below.

  6. Inspect and hand back

    The silo is inspected with your engineer. Manholes are closed, isolations are returned and the permit is cancelled.

For heavy or dangerous build-up we work with specialist cleaning teams and provide the confined-space support, access, lifting and mechanical work around them.

A clean, empty silo is a rare opportunity. With the plant’s agreement we use it.

The environment

Corrosion engineers grade atmospheres by how fast they eat steel. The international standard ISO 12944 runs from C1 to C5 and beyond. A coastal site with salt in the air sits at the severe end of that scale.

A coating system chosen for an inland plant will not last here. The system is selected for the environment and for the years of life you want before the first major repaint.

A coating system has three jobs

Primer
Grips the steel and protects it directly. Zinc-rich primers protect even where the film is scratched.
Intermediate coats
Build thickness. Thickness is the barrier that keeps water, oxygen and salt away from the steel.
Finish coat
Resists sunlight and weather, and carries the colour.

How we paint

  1. Prepare the surface

    The most important step by a distance. Rust, mill scale, old paint, oil and salt are removed, by abrasive blasting to the specified standard or by power tools where blasting is not possible.

  2. Paint the same day

    Blasted steel in this air starts to bloom within hours. The primer goes on before it can.

  3. Watch the weather

    No painting on wet steel, or when the steel is cooler than the dew point of the air around it. Paint applied over condensation fails from beneath.

  4. Apply each coat to thickness

    In the number of coats specified. Edges, welds and bolts get an extra stripe coat by brush, because that is where films are thinnest and rust begins.

  5. Measure

    Dry film thickness is measured with a gauge and recorded. A coat that looks complete can be half the thickness it should be.

  6. Repair damage

    Erection scars, weld burns and scratches are prepared and built back up to the full system.

Colours that mean something

In a plant, colour is information. Pipes are painted and banded so that anyone can tell water from air from fuel. Moving parts, hazards, fire equipment and safe routes each have their colour.

Indian plants specify these by shade number from the IS 5 colour chart, whose shades correspond to the British BS 381C range. Golden Yellow is 356. Signal Red is 537. Light Admiralty Grey, the colour of a great deal of Indian machinery, is 697. Pipe identification follows IS 2379.

We paint to the plant’s schedule, shade for shade.

This website is painted to the same schedule. The blue of these headings is Oxford Blue, 105. Anything you can press is Golden Yellow, 356, the colour of a handrail.

Contractors based in distant cities work with mobilisation windows of six to twelve hours. Our teams, and our partners’ machines, are embedded inside the industrial zone. That compression of geography becomes a compression of time.

During one kiln breakdown at a major cement plant, our civil and mechanical teams were on site within 25 minutes of the call. A competitor mobilising from outside the belt would have needed at least five hours. The plant resumed production eight hours ahead of its projected recovery.

This is not an anecdote. It is the predictable outcome of being local on purpose.

What we are called for

Mechanical failures
Jammed gates, failed supports, torn ducts and chutes, broken structures, urgent fabrication.
Civil failures
Cracked foundations, collapsed drains, washed-out roads, a wall that has moved.
Urgent excavation
A trench or pit that must exist by morning, in rock if need be.
Lifting
A crane, a rigger and a plan, at short notice.
Hands
A shift of fitters, welders or riggers when your own crew is not enough.
Clearing
Spillage, debris and blockage that stand between you and a restart.
Movement
A machine or a load that must be somewhere else tonight.

The first thirty minutes

  1. Minute 0. The call

    One number. A person, not a recording. We ask five things: which plant and gate, where inside, what has happened, what you need first, and who to ask for.

  2. Minutes 1 to 5. Three calls go out

    To a supervisor who lives near your gate and knows your plant. To an owner whose machine is parked close by. To the crew.

  3. Minutes 5 to 30. Convergence

    Nobody is loading a trailer in a distant city. People and machines move a few kilometres.

  4. On arrival. The permit, before the tool

    Our supervisor reports to your shift in-charge. The hazard is assessed and the permit to work is raised. The toolbox talk happens under floodlights.

  5. From then on. One voice

    Your control room receives short, factual updates from one person. It does not receive requests for decisions the contractor ought to be making.

The full sequence, with what we need from your side, is on The emergency protocol.

Urgency is not recklessness

The emergencies that turn into tragedies are the ones where somebody decided there was no time for the permit, the gas test or the harness.

At ATKAYVA there is always time for this. If the job is inside a silo or a cyclone, confined-space entry rules apply in full, at midnight exactly as they would at noon. Our supervisors have the authority to refuse an unsafe instruction, whoever gives it.

After the emergency

When the plant is running again, three things follow.

  • A report. What failed, what was done, what was used, and what we would look at before it fails again.
  • An invoice. For what was used, at rates that were known before the night began if you hold a rate contract with us.
  • No drama at all.

A suggestion

Agree call-out rates and gate formalities with us before you need them. A plant that has done so saves the first twenty minutes of every emergency.
